provenance.sourceTitle: Cambridge International AS & A Level Biology 9700 syllabus, 2028–2030
provenance.sourceUse: Assessment skill coverage and terminology only. The questions, datasets, mark points and contexts in this practice set are original and are not Cambridge past-paper questions.

assessmentNotice: Original practice material. Practice mark allocations and mark points are author-created, are not official Cambridge mark schemes, and must not be presented as predictions of examination questions.

tasks.title: Catalase activity and temperature
tasks.format: Investigation design, data handling and evaluation
tasks.scenario: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the rate at which catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide. The student uses a fixed volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide, a fixed volume of catalase solution and measures the volume of oxygen collected in 60 seconds.

questions.prompt: State the independent variable and dependent variable. Give the unit for the dependent variable.
answer: Independent variable: temperature of the reaction mixture, in °C.
Dependent variable: volume of oxygen collected in 60 s, in cm³.

questions.prompt: Suggest a suitable set of at least five temperature values covering a useful range. Explain why the intervals should be appropriate.
answer: One suitable set is 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C.
Values span a range likely to show a trend and possible decline at high temperature.
Equal 10 °C intervals make comparison straightforward.
The range should avoid unsafe heating and should be refined if preliminary results show the optimum is outside it.
questions.notes: Other scientifically justified sets earn credit.

questions.prompt: Describe five variables that should be controlled and how each should be kept constant.
answer: Hydrogen peroxide concentration and volume: use the same stock solution and measured volume.
Catalase concentration and volume: use the same prepared batch and measured volume.
Reaction time: start timing at the same defined point and stop after 60 s.
pH: use the same buffer at the same pH and volume.
Total reaction volume/apparatus: use the same vessel and gas-collection arrangement.
Allow solutions to reach the target temperature before mixing.
questions.notes: Award credit for a control paired with a workable method.

questions.prompt: Explain why repeats are needed and propose a suitable number of repeats at each temperature.
answer: Repeat each temperature at least three times.
Repeats reveal variation and help identify anomalous results.
Calculate a mean from concordant results.
Investigate or justify excluding an anomalous result rather than silently deleting it.

questions.prompt: Construct a results table suitable for recording the investigation.
answer: First column identifies temperature / °C.
Separate columns show each repeat and the mean oxygen volume / cm³.
Units appear in headings, not repeated in every cell.
Values are recorded to consistent precision and raw data are distinguishable from calculated values.

questions.prompt: Describe the graph that should be drawn and how the data should be presented.
answer: Temperature / °C on the x-axis.
Mean oxygen volume in 60 s / cm³ on the y-axis.
Linear scales use most of the available grid and have labelled axes with units.
Plot points accurately and draw a suitable best-fit line or smooth curve; do not join points dot-to-dot without justification.

questions.prompt: Give two limitations and a practical improvement for each.
answer: Temperature may change during reaction: use a thermostatically controlled water bath and pre-equilibrate solutions.
Gas may leak: check airtight connections and use a gas syringe with a secure seal.
Manual timing or mixing causes variation: standardise mixing and use the same timing trigger, or use a sensor/data logger.
Enzyme activity may vary between preparations: use one well-mixed enzyme batch and consistent storage.

questions.prompt: State a conclusion that could be supported if the mean oxygen volume rises to 40 °C and then falls at higher temperatures.
answer: Rate/activity increases with temperature up to around 40 °C, then decreases.
The decrease at higher temperatures is consistent with enzyme denaturation, but the data alone do not prove the molecular mechanism.

markingGuide.principle: Use the mark points as a self-check, not as an official Cambridge mark scheme. Credit equivalent valid methods and correctly justified alternatives.

tasks.title: Microscope drawing and scale calculation
tasks.scenario: A prepared plant tissue slide is viewed under a light microscope. The field of view is calibrated using a stage micrometer. A representative cell measures 36 mm on a printed photomicrograph. The actual cell length is 120 µm.

questions.prompt: Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph. Show the unit conversion and working.
answer: Convert 36 mm to 36 000 µm.
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
Magnification has no units.

questions.prompt: Describe four features of a high-quality biological drawing of the observed tissue.
answer: Use clear, single, continuous lines.
Draw large, accurate outlines with correct proportions.
Do not use shading or sketching.
Use straight ruled label lines that touch the correct structure and do not cross.
Include a suitable title and scale information where required.

questions.prompt: Explain why the drawing should represent the observed specimen rather than an idealised textbook cell.
answer: It must record actual observable features.
It should preserve relative sizes and proportions.
It should not add structures that cannot be seen or were not observed.

questions.prompt: Give three precautions when using a light microscope to obtain a clear image.
answer: Begin with low-power objective and focus before increasing magnification.
Use coarse focus only at low power; use fine focus at high power.
Adjust illumination/diaphragm and centre the specimen.
Handle slides carefully and avoid allowing the objective lens to strike the slide.

markingGuide.principle: Magnification is image size divided by actual size, with both sizes in the same units. Drawing criteria are practice guidance, not an official mark scheme.

tasks.title: Planning an investigation into light intensity and photosynthesis
tasks.format: Written planning, data analysis and evaluation
tasks.scenario: A student plans to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in an aquatic plant. The student can vary the distance of a lamp from the plant and can collect oxygen in a gas syringe. The lamp may also heat the water.

questions.prompt: Write a prediction and a linked biological hypothesis.
answer: Prediction: as light intensity increases, the rate of oxygen production will increase initially and may eventually level off.
Hypothesis: increasing light intensity increases the rate of the light-dependent reactions until another factor becomes limiting.
The prediction is measurable and the hypothesis gives a biological explanation.

questions.prompt: Identify the independent and dependent variables and explain how each should be measured.
answer: Independent variable: light intensity, measured with a light meter at the plant; distance can be changed to alter intensity but distance is only a proxy.
Dependent variable: rate of oxygen production, measured as oxygen volume per unit time using a gas syringe.
Use a fixed measurement interval after allowing the plant to acclimatise.
Record the actual light intensity rather than relying only on lamp distance where a light meter is available.

questions.prompt: Describe a method that produces reliable, comparable results.
answer: Use the same species and similar lengths of healthy aquatic plant.
Place the plant at measured light intensities, allowing it to acclimatise at each level.
Measure oxygen volume over the same timed interval.
Repeat each intensity at least three times and calculate a mean rate.
Keep carbon dioxide availability, pH, plant length, water volume and measurement time constant.
Randomise or alternate intensity order if drift over time is likely.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would control the heating effect of the lamp and identify one other relevant control.
answer: Use a heat filter, LED lamp or water bath to minimise heating.
Monitor and maintain water temperature with a thermometer or thermostatic bath.
Keep dissolved carbon dioxide availability constant, for example with the same buffer concentration and volume.

questions.prompt: State two safety risks and suitable precautions.
answer: Electrical equipment near water: keep connections dry, use low-voltage equipment and keep the power supply away from spills.
Hot lamp or water: allow equipment to cool and handle hot apparatus carefully.
Glassware/gas syringe breakage: secure apparatus and handle glass carefully.
questions.notes: Any two correctly paired risk and precaution points.

questions.prompt: The mean oxygen production rates are shown below. Calculate the percentage increase from 20 to 40 arbitrary light-intensity units and identify the trend.
answer: Percentage increase = ((3.6 − 2.4) ÷ 2.4) × 100 = 50%.
Rate increases as light intensity rises, but the increase becomes smaller at higher intensities.
The results suggest the response is approaching a plateau; another factor may become limiting.

questions.prompt: Describe an appropriate graph and one way to show variation between repeats.
answer: Plot light intensity on the x-axis and mean oxygen production rate on the y-axis.
Use labelled axes with units and a suitable scale.
Show variation using range bars or another justified measure of spread; state what the bars represent.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the method by identifying two limitations and explaining improvements.
answer: Distance from a lamp does not directly measure intensity and may not give a linear change; measure intensity at the plant with a light meter.
Oxygen may dissolve in water or leak; use a sealed, checked collection system and allow consistent equilibration.
Photosynthesis may change with time; standardise acclimatisation and randomise treatment order.
Plant samples differ; use comparable material and repeat with independent specimens.

markingGuide.principle: Practice mark allocation is original. A valid plan must be sufficiently detailed for another student to repeat and must distinguish the measured light intensity from lamp distance.

tasks.title: Osmosis in plant tissue
tasks.format: Quantitative investigation, percentage change and interpretation
tasks.scenario: A student investigates how sucrose concentration affects the mass of potato cylinders. Equal-sized cylinders are blotted dry and weighed before being placed in sucrose solutions for the same period. They are then removed, blotted in a standardised way and reweighed.

questions.prompt: Identify the independent and dependent variables. State how the dependent variable should be expressed so that cylinders with slightly different starting masses can be compared.
answer: Independent variable: sucrose concentration / mol dm⁻³.
Dependent variable: change in mass of each potato cylinder.
Calculate percentage change in mass using ((final mass − initial mass) ÷ initial mass) × 100.

questions.prompt: Suggest a suitable range of at least five sucrose concentrations and explain why the range should include values on both sides of the isotonic concentration.
answer: Use at least five concentrations, for example 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol dm⁻³.
Use equal intervals where practical to make trends easier to compare.
Include concentrations expected to cause mass gain and mass loss.
A range on both sides helps estimate the concentration at which there is no net mass change.

questions.prompt: Describe four variables that should be controlled and how each should be standardised.
answer: Use cylinders from the same potato variety or tuber where possible.
Cut cylinders to the same length and diameter using the same cutter.
Keep immersion time the same for every cylinder.
Use the same volume of solution and ensure each cylinder is fully immersed.
Maintain the same temperature and blot each cylinder using the same method and duration.

questions.prompt: Explain why at least three potato cylinders should be tested at each concentration.
answer: Replicates reveal biological and measurement variation.
A mean percentage change can be calculated for each concentration.
Variation or anomalous results can be identified and investigated rather than silently discarded.

questions.prompt: Construct a suitable results table. Include raw measurements and the calculated dependent variable.
answer: Include sucrose concentration / mol dm⁻³ in the first column.
Record initial and final mass for each replicate, with units such as g.
Include percentage change in mass for each replicate.
Include mean percentage change for each concentration; distinguish raw and calculated data and use consistent precision.

questions.prompt: A cylinder has an initial mass of 2.50 g and a final mass of 2.20 g. Calculate its percentage change in mass and show your working.
answer: Change in mass = 2.20 − 2.50 = −0.30 g.
Percentage change = (−0.30 ÷ 2.50) × 100.
Percentage change = −12%.
The negative sign indicates a decrease in mass.

questions.prompt: Describe the graph to plot and explain how the isotonic concentration can be estimated.
answer: Plot sucrose concentration / mol dm⁻³ on the x-axis and mean percentage change in mass / % on the y-axis.
Use an appropriate scale, labelled axes and accurately plotted points.
Estimate the isotonic concentration where the best-fit line or curve crosses 0% change in mass.

questions.prompt: Explain the biological basis of the expected pattern and give one limitation with an improvement.
answer: In a dilute solution, water enters potato cells by osmosis and mass tends to increase.
In a concentrated solution, water leaves cells and mass tends to decrease.
A limitation is inconsistent blotting or tissue size; standardise blotting and use a cork borer and cutting guide to produce comparable cylinders.

markingGuide.principle: Practice mark allocation and answer points are original, not an official Cambridge mark scheme. The isotonic concentration is estimated from zero percentage change, not assumed to be the concentration of a particular prepared solution.

tasks.title: Effect of pH on amylase activity
tasks.format: Enzyme investigation, colorimetry-style endpoint and rate comparison
tasks.scenario: A student investigates the effect of pH on the activity of amylase breaking down starch. At set time intervals, a drop of reaction mixture is added to iodine solution. The student records the time at which the iodine no longer turns blue-black. Temperature, enzyme concentration and starch concentration can be controlled.

questions.prompt: Identify the independent and dependent variables. Explain why the endpoint time can be used to compare enzyme activity.
answer: Independent variable: pH of the reaction mixture / buffer.
Dependent variable: time taken for starch to no longer be detected by iodine.
For the same initial starch concentration and fixed conditions, a shorter endpoint time indicates a faster rate of starch breakdown.

questions.prompt: Suggest at least five pH values for the investigation and explain how the range could be improved after preliminary work.
answer: A suitable initial range could be pH 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9.
Use buffer solutions to establish and maintain each pH.
The range should cover acidic, near-neutral and alkaline conditions likely to reveal a maximum.
If preliminary results place the maximum near an endpoint, test additional pH values around that region using smaller intervals.

questions.prompt: Describe a method that gives comparable endpoint measurements at each pH.
answer: Prepare equal volumes of starch solution and amylase solution at the same concentrations.
Use a buffer of known pH and keep its volume consistent.
Allow solutions to reach the same controlled temperature before mixing.
Start the timer immediately after mixing and use the same sampling interval throughout.
Add each sample to a fresh, equal volume of iodine solution using the same drop volume.
Use the same criterion for deciding that the blue-black colour has disappeared.
questions.notes: Credit requires a clear, repeatable sequence and a defined endpoint.

questions.prompt: State four variables, other than pH, that should be controlled and how each should be kept constant.
answer: Temperature: use a thermostatically controlled water bath and pre-equilibrate solutions.
Starch concentration and volume: use the same prepared stock and measured volume.
Amylase concentration and volume: use the same enzyme stock and measured volume.
Sampling interval and sample volume: use a timer and consistent pipette/dropper technique.
Iodine concentration and volume: use the same iodine solution and equal volumes.

questions.prompt: Explain why the student should repeat each pH measurement and how to deal with an anomalous endpoint time.
answer: Repeat each pH condition at least three times to assess variation.
Calculate a mean from concordant results and compare spread between repeats.
Check an anomalous result for procedural error and repeat the measurement; do not remove it without justification.

questions.prompt: The endpoint times at pH 5 are 42 s, 39 s and 45 s. Calculate the mean endpoint time and the relative rate using 1 ÷ mean time. Give the rate to three significant figures.
answer: Relative rate = 1 ÷ 42.
Relative rate = 0.0238 s⁻¹ to three significant figures.
This is a relative rate based on endpoint time, not a direct measurement of product concentration per unit time.

questions.prompt: Describe a suitable graph for comparing enzyme activity at different pH values.
answer: Plot pH on the x-axis.
Plot relative rate (1 ÷ mean endpoint time) on the y-axis, with its unit or definition stated clearly.
Use a suitable scale, accurately plotted points and a smooth best-fit curve where justified; identify the pH with the highest measured activity.

questions.prompt: Evaluate two limitations of this method and suggest improvements.
answer: The colour endpoint is judged by eye and may be subjective; use a colorimeter or standardised visual comparison if suitable equipment is available.
Sampling at intervals gives limited time resolution; use shorter, consistent intervals near the endpoint.
Temperature may drift; use a thermostatically controlled water bath and monitor it.
pH may change during reaction; use an adequate buffer and check pH before and after the reaction.

markingGuide.principle: These are original practice mark points, not an official Cambridge mark scheme. A shorter endpoint time indicates faster starch breakdown only when starting concentrations, sampling procedure and other conditions are comparable.

tasks.title: Investigating water uptake with a potometer
tasks.format: Plant transport investigation, rate measurement and experimental evaluation
tasks.scenario: A student uses a bubble potometer to investigate how air movement affects water uptake by a leafy shoot. The shoot is cut and assembled under water, the apparatus is sealed, and the distance moved by an air bubble is measured over a fixed time. The student understands that water uptake is an estimate of transpiration rate, not a direct measurement of water vapour loss.

questions.prompt: Identify the independent and dependent variables for an investigation of air movement. State a suitable unit for the dependent variable.
answer: Independent variable: air movement / wind speed around the leaves.
Dependent variable: rate of bubble movement or water uptake, for example mm min⁻¹ or mm³ min⁻¹ if capillary dimensions are known.
Measure bubble displacement over a fixed time, or calculate volume uptake from capillary cross-sectional area and displacement.

questions.prompt: Describe how to set up the potometer so that measurements are valid and the apparatus does not leak.
answer: Cut the shoot under water to reduce air entering the xylem.
Insert the shoot into the apparatus while submerged and assemble the apparatus under water where appropriate.
Ensure all joints are airtight and seal connections with suitable material.
Introduce a single air bubble into the capillary and check that it moves freely; allow the shoot to acclimatise before recording.

questions.prompt: State four variables that should be controlled while investigating air movement and explain how to control them.
answer: Light intensity: use the same lamp position and intensity throughout.
Temperature: monitor and maintain a constant room or chamber temperature.
Humidity: keep humidity constant and measure it if possible.
Leaf area: use the same shoot throughout or shoots with comparable total leaf area.
Measurement duration: use identical timing intervals at every air movement setting.

questions.prompt: Suggest a suitable range of at least five air movement settings and explain why the order of testing may matter.
answer: Use at least five measured wind speeds spanning still air to a stronger, safe airflow, for example 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 m s⁻¹ if the apparatus permits.
Measure air speed at leaf level rather than relying only on fan settings.
Randomise or alternate the order where possible because the shoot may change condition over time.

questions.prompt: A bubble moves 18 mm in 6 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of bubble movement. If the capillary has a cross-sectional area of 0.50 mm², calculate the volume of water uptake per minute.
answer: Rate of movement = 18 ÷ 6 = 3.0 mm min⁻¹.
Volume moved in 6 minutes = distance × cross-sectional area.
Volume = 18 × 0.50 = 9.0 mm³.
Volume uptake rate = 9.0 ÷ 6 = 1.5 mm³ min⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Explain why a potometer measures water uptake rather than directly measuring transpiration rate.
answer: Some absorbed water is used in photosynthesis, growth and maintaining cell turgidity.
Not all water taken up is necessarily lost as water vapour during the measurement period.
Therefore water uptake is an estimate or proxy for transpiration, not a direct measurement of water loss.

questions.prompt: Explain the expected effect of increasing air movement on transpiration and identify a condition under which the trend might become less pronounced.
answer: Moving air removes the humid boundary layer around leaves.
This maintains a steep water vapour concentration gradient between the leaf air spaces and surrounding air, increasing transpiration.
The effect may become less pronounced if another factor, such as light intensity or stomatal opening, limits transpiration, or if water supply becomes limiting.

questions.prompt: Evaluate two limitations of a potometer investigation and suggest practical improvements.
answer: Leaks or changes in bubble size affect readings; check airtight seals and reset the bubble consistently.
Leaf area differs between shoots; use the same shoot for all treatments or measure and standardise leaf area.
The shoot may change during a long experiment; randomise treatment order and allow consistent acclimatisation.
Air speed may vary across the leaves; measure it at several positions near the shoot and keep fan distance fixed.

markingGuide.principle: Practice marks and guidance are original, not an official Cambridge mark scheme. Potometer water uptake is an estimate of transpiration and must not be described as a direct measurement of transpiration.

attemptOrder: Read the scenario and underline the command words.
Check units, variables, controls and whether each method step is repeatable.
Compare with the answer points and record missed skills.
Retry the question from a blank page after feedback.
selfAssessment: I identified variables precisely and gave units.
I selected a justified range with at least five values where an investigation requires it.
I described repeats, controls and standardisation.
My method is detailed enough to reproduce.
My table and graph have correct headings, units and scales.
My conclusion is supported by the data.
My evaluation links a limitation to a practical improvement.
